regions.cleaned_text: To know is to appreciate - is to love what is good - is to reject what is of evil - is to adore the Divine. What consolation this offers us! What a hopeful outlook it ought to afford! What a sublime horizon for poor sinners, -- if "hope is the very soul of happiness here" and if the revealed purpose of our creation, TO KNOW GOD is kept in mind -- what a horizon for us, even though we be sinners -- if we but keep in mind the primary purpose of our creation, TO KNOW GOD. Hence the lines: God made me to know Him. O what a bless'd aim! To love Him and serve Him sure rests in the same. Its "Heaven Begun" for the grateful on earth; -- To treasure aright? ! Highest Heaven its worth. But how can I know what the senses fail to perceive? How know the Incomprehensible God whose attributes - wisdom and power and goodnes and mercy-are infinite? A simple question may, in the first place, demand a simple answer. But right here, we shall do well to rem- ember a trite proverb: "A fool can ask questions - can make ob- jections - that will puzzle a philosopher to answer." A nave of course, can ask such questions too. But perhaps the nave is sup- posed to be included in the proverb; because after all, in asmuch as anyone is a nave in at least somuch does he prove himself in the end to have been a fool too. While it would be uncharitable, therefore, to say that every fool is a nave' it is always logical; to say that every nave is a fool. However, a simple answer to the above objection intimating the difficulty or impossibility of a finit creature knowing the infinite God, might be to ask another very simple question; viz. Do the senses perceive the electricity - "the juice" in a live wire? Or again: Do men gaze into the sun to consider its bene- fits? Objections like the above are futal and vain and if meant to excuse athesim, are criminal. For there is absolutely no ex- cuse for any rational creature refusing to recognize its Creator. In fact, if "Gratitude for favors is one or the very first and surest indications of intelligence", and again if according to all logical reasoning, one's first possible benefit is his crea- tion; then the ingratitude of the atheist, must of its very nat- ure - without further proof or parley - condemn him with his
